newsitem.title: USA: White House uncertain when to release new document.
newsitem.headline: White House uncertain when to release new document.

text.p: Bracing for fresh embarrassment, the White House said on Friday it was not sure whether or when to release new campaign documents, one of which proposed that U.S. President Bill Clinton offer trips on Air Force One to potential political donors.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said documents were sent to a congressional committee investigating Democratic Party fund raising by former deputy chief of staff Harold Ickes included some material that detailed internal party matters that ought to be kept confidential.
"We will look and see exactly what he (Ickes) has produced and see if we're in a position to disclose it. I don't know the answer at this point," McCurry said.

"We'll look and see what his attorneys have actually produced and then see if there's anything that we can do with it to continue to make available and public the information that the president wants the American public to have on the subject," he said.

The White House this week released several hundred pages of documents supplied to the committe by Ickes. One showed Clinton approving a proposal to invite top party donors to spend the night at the White House.

The new batch of documents, said to number as many as 5,000 pages, includes one suggesting other perks that could be given to donors, including the opportunity to take trips on Air Force One, the presidential airplane.
McCurry confirmed the existence of the document but said several of the fund-raising ideas it contained were never put into effect.
"The document you're asking about I'm not familiar enough with to discuss at any great length. It's not clear who created the document or how it came to be in Mr. Ickes' possession," McCurry said.

"As to what we have done in helping encourage people to contribute, I think a lot of that you know. It's on the public record, and obviously, some of the things that are listed in this one document did happen. Others didn't happen," he said.
Ickes had hoped to be appointed White House Chief of Staff but the job went to Erskine Bowles, and he left the administration. He has denied he was angry at Clinton for being overlooked.
In a separate development, Clinton's Democratic Party announced it was returning $1.5 million in 1996 campaign donations that were either illegal, inappropriate or questionable.

The announcement raised to nearly $3 million the amount the Democrats have returned to donors, many of them linked to Asian business sources, since Clinton was re-elected last November as part of a growing campaign financing controversy.

Four investigations into financing activities are under way, including whether the governments of China or other countries attempted to influence U.S. policy. A federal grand jury probing the issue under the direction of a Justice Department task force heard testimony Friday from a woman who refused to identify herself to reporters afterwards.
Committees from the House of Representatives, the Senate and the Federal Election Commission are investigating reports of wrongdoing in the 1996 election campaign.
